name: PT Sumber Alfaria Trijaya Tbk

frontmatter.title: Alfamart: a growth franchise priced for a store cap that does not yet exist
frontmatter.summary: The 11 November statement removes the permit-moratorium overhang, so the earnings case stands, but the valuation is rebuilt: house STAPLES_RETAIL weights and five covered-peer multiples replace the override, MIDI leaves the peer median as a consolidated subsidiary, terminal growth is cut and the terminal year reinvests at the cost of capital, and the minority is revalued at its share of the DCF. BUY is retained on a lower target, with de-rating supplying most of the return.
thesis: The 10 November recap puts nine-month revenue at IDR101,000.0bn and net profit at IDR2,400.0bn, which is the attributable line of IDR2,402.8bn up 3.8% — figures the September accounts already carry [S12][S3].

Expansion is policy-clear: 1,081 net new Alfamart stores in 2025 and a 800 target for 2026, with the coordinating food minister stating on 11 November that no permit moratorium exists and the cooperatives are not retailers [S13], against one regency enforcing a rule that predates the plan [S11].
Last-actual economics are stable: gross margin held at 21.9% through FY2025 and the first nine months of FY2026, operating margin 3.6% on the restated basis.
The de-rating did the damage, not the earnings: 10.8x forward earnings and 3.9x EV/EBITDA against a five-year average in the high twenties.
Net cash, negative working capital and a 50.0% payout support a 4.6% yield while the growth is re-priced; IDR532.8bn of shares were bought back in the nine months to September [S3].
Base-case intrinsic value Rp1,037 a share, probability-weighted twelve-month target Rp1,189; the bear case's twelve-month value is Rp567, well below today's price, and is the honest downside.

blocks.text: **BUY, target Rp1,189 (28.5% total return), base-case intrinsic value Rp1,037 against a share price of Rp960.** Two things changed. The regulatory overhang eased: at the national retail day the coordinating food minister stated plainly that there is no moratorium on new retail permits and that the village cooperative programme is infrastructure for subsidised goods, not a supermarket competing with modern stores [S13]. That strengthens the base case of continued expansion and takes the regulatory leg out of the bear case. The valuation also changed, because the review was right on five points: the override weights, the bull's terminal-growth breach, the perpetual excess return the terminal value still capitalised, the minority deduction and the working-capital stress. We now carry the house STAPLES_RETAIL weights on five covered peers with MIDI excluded as a subsidiary the group controls and consolidates, terminal growth at 4.0%, a terminal year that reinvests at the cost of capital so the fade reaches the value rather than stopping at the growth rate, the minority at its share of the DCF instead of book, a working-capital shock in the bear and a bear growth path at or below CPI. The earnings forecasts change only where the review showed the model was inconsistent: gross margin now carries the Q4 seasonality we already apply to opex, so FY2026E EBITDA is IDR9,687.0bn rather than the nine-month run rate.

The report adds one genuine piece of analysis, and it is not flattering: Midi grew nine-month net profit 19.4% against 3.8% at Alfamart, on the ready-to-eat and ready-to-drink mix of the Lawson format [S12]. MIDI is not an independent challenger — AMRT owns 77.1% of it and consolidates it [S4 p.24] — so this is within-group format mix, not share lost to a competitor; it is still the reason we do not claim the moat is widening, and it stays in the bear case. The rest — a stable staple basket, additions beyond Java, a year-end push, a cost warning on logistics and food inflation — is the environment we model [S12].

The overhang itself is two-sided. It began with the February call by the villages minister to stop new minimarket permits, quickly narrowed to new permits only [S7]; one regency closed outlets under a distance rule in force since 2021 [S11]; the MSCI deletion removed the passive bid [S8]; and on 11 November the coordinating food minister denied any moratorium and recast the cooperatives as subsidy infrastructure [S13].

Our variant view is narrow. A national cap on new stores is the most damaging thing that could happen to this model and it is the bear case; the evidence so far is rhetoric plus local enforcement of pre-existing rules, while the plan and nine-month revenue assume expansion continues [S5][S3]. The 11 November statement goes further: the cooperatives are a subsidy-delivery channel, not a competitor, and the retailers' association reads them as a potential partner [S13]. Three judgements carry the thesis: the programme runs at pace, gross margin holds, and the DCF is right.

Sumber Alfaria Trijaya runs the Alfamart minimarket chain and adjacent retail formats in Indonesia [S6]. At end-FY2025 it operated 24,434 outlets, of which 21,120 trade under the Alfamart banner, with 175,177 employees [S6]. It added 1,081 net new Alfamart stores in 2025 and guided to 800 net additions in 2026 across Indonesia [S5]; the director's own wording is that the target is net — "total net dari jumlah gerai yang akan kita buka" — and the November article describes the same programme as measured and including areas outside Java [S5][S12].

The mix is food with a non-food tail: food produced IDR72,140.0bn of nine-month revenue against IDR29,140.0bn from non-food, the food segment growing 8.0% against 5.4% for non-food, so food is gaining share [S9] — it carries the traffic and the supplier funding, non-food the ticket. Operating profit also carries recurring other operating income of IDR1,333.7bn in FY2025 — payment fees, space rental, franchise administration, registration — which we treat as operating, earned every year of the record [S4].

The model is cash-generative in a way that is easy to miss: suppliers fund the shelf, so operating working capital is negative and growth releases cash [S0]. Most stores are leased: right-of-use depreciation of IDR2,492.1bn exceeds owned fixed-asset depreciation of IDR1,786.3bn [S4].

Abroad, Alfamart runs in the Philippines through a 35.0% associate with 2,700 stores, plus a small Bangladesh presence and a Vietnam entry guided for late 2026 or early 2027 [S10][S4]. Equity-accounted, so none of its earnings are in our cash flow; its carrying value of IDR348.7bn sits in the valuation bridge [S4].

Control sits with PT Sigmantara Alfindo at 50.2%, the founding family behind it and on the board [S6]. Alfagift, the loyalty and ordering platform, had 29 million members at end-2025 [S5]. Strategy is store expansion, supply-chain optimisation, then digital [S6].

Indonesian minimarket retail is a duopoly — Alfamart and Indomaret national, a long tail below [S2]. The leaders compete store by store on location, hours and promotion, and buy from the same manufacturers, so gross margins converge [S2]. The question is how much format is left and how much value the state reallocates.

That question became live in 2026. The Minister of Villages argued new minimarket permits should stop so village cooperatives are not undercut, then clarified he meant new permits, not closures [S7]. On 11 November the coordinating food minister stated plainly that no moratorium on new permits exists and that the cooperatives are infrastructure for subsidised goods, not retail [S13]; the retailers' association welcomed the certainty and called them potential partners [S13]. Permits are issued by regencies, so the instrument is blunt: Lombok Tengah applied its own distance rule and the operators closed the offending outlets [S11].

Competition inside the group is the more informative signal, but it is not challenger data. MIDI — PT Midi Utama Indonesia, 77.1% owned and consolidated by AMRT [S4 p.24] — grew nine-month net profit 19.4% against 3.8% at the Alfamart banner, and revenue 9.2% against 7.2% [S12][S9]. Read correctly, that is a within-group format mix shift toward the Lawson ready-to-eat and ready-to-drink offer: it tells us the group's growth is rotating between formats, not that a local competitor is taking share, and it is exactly why we do not claim the moat is widening and instead fade the terminal return to the cost of capital in the valuation. The external evidence of the moat is thinner than the thesis would like — a duopoly structure and store density [S2][S6], no independent market-share series and no GT/MT mix in the source set — so we treat the moat as durable (supplier-funded shelf, negative working capital, distribution density) and explicitly not widening. It is consistent with our flat gross margin: Alfamart's 22.2% is a grocery mix funded by supplier terms, and we assume no move, so we do not capitalise Midi's margin. It bears on the bear case, where a format that cannot add fresh-food margin competes on price and location — the path in which a hundred basis points of gross margin go to promotion — and it explains why group profit growth is shared below the operating line [S3].

The moat is distribution density: warehouses and branch offices that double as depots place a case of water at a village outlet at a landed cost an independent shop cannot match [S6]. It is not a consignment model: the group carried IDR13,613.3bn of inventory at 30 September 2026 and IDR13,415.0bn before the obsolescence allowance at the FY2025 year end, and the adequacy of that allowance is the auditor's key audit matter [S3][S4]. Negative working capital comes from supplier credit terms — current non-debt liabilities exceed inventory — not from suppliers owning the stock until it is scanned. Durable against entrants, weak against location rules. Supplier power low, buyer power moderate, entry threat low, substitutes moderate, rivalry high [S2].

Demand is the constraint nobody can legislate away. Purchasing power is weak and the listed retail names reporting in November described trade-down [S2], yet revenue reached IDR101,288.2bn in the first nine months, ahead of last year [S3], and the 10 November article says the same qualitatively [S12]. For a format selling rice, oil and soap, weak real income compresses basket size, not visit frequency [S2]. Regulation cuts both ways: medicines sales are now allowed, a higher-margin adjacency [S6].

Revenue compounded from IDR96,924.7bn in FY2022 to IDR126,737.3bn in FY2025, decelerating to 7.2% as the base matured [S4]. The nine months to September reached IDR101,288.2bn, ahead of last year, so deceleration stopped [S3]; the November restatement is the same number [S12]. We model 7.2% for FY2026E, then 7.0% fading to 6.1%: 800 net new stores on 21,120 banner outlets is roughly three per cent of the estate before like-for-like, and the fade is arithmetic [S5][S9]. No source caps the programme.

Gross margin on a full-year basis was 21.5% in FY2024 and 21.9% in FY2025, and we carry 22.2% for FY2026E [S4][S3]. The nine-month rate is not the full-year rate: the format earns a recurring fourth-quarter uplift in gross margin, the same seasonality we already apply to opex, so the forecast blends the 9M2026 actual with a fourth quarter at the FY2025 seasonal level rather than holding the nine-month rate flat. On the nine-month rate the model would understate FY2026E EBITDA by the fourth-quarter margin differential; the sensitivity table shows what a point of gross margin is worth. Mix shifts toward food, marginally higher-margin on supplier funding, but promotion caps the upside.

The operating-expense line decides the argument, and other operating income sits above it. Net of that income the ratio was lower in FY2025 than in the first nine months of FY2026, as wages and ramp costs bit [S4][S3]. We hold 18.6%, the nine-month actual blended with the fourth quarter's seasonally lower ratio rather than extrapolating the creep for a decade; the blend leaves the full-year margin below FY2025's and keeps the calibration gap auditable [S3][S4]. With gross margin at 22.2%, operating margin is 3.6% against 3.6% in FY2025, a shade above [S3]; the error sits in the bear case, where the ratio rises half a point.

Operating margin is 3.6% in FY2025 and 3.6% in FY2026E, EBITDA IDR9,063.7bn growing to IDR9,687.0bn [S4]. Right-of-use depreciation alone was IDR2,492.1bn, which is why EBITDA flatters this business and why we value free cash flow after capex of IDR4,994.7bn, held near that share of revenue [S4].

Below the operating line the year is not a repeat of FY2025, and the model says so on the accounts' own rates. Finance cost was IDR127.2bn in the nine months, annualising to about the IDR169.7bn we carry against IDR137.3bn in FY2025 [S3][S4]; that charge covers bank and lease interest at the LK's rate, not the 9.4% marginal rate used in the cost of capital. Other non-operating items are held at IDR-81.0bn, the nine-month run rate annualised, rather than FY2025's heavier associate loss [S3][S4].

The earnings path follows: nine-month earnings per share of Rp58, a full-year Rp89 against Rp82 [S3]. Attributable profit of IDR3,653.3bn is a little above FY2025's IDR3,410.9bn on revenue growth of 7.2%, even after the operating-expense ratio of 18.6% and the minority take of 6.1% against about four per cent [S3][S4].

Cash conversion is the strongest part of the record: operating cash flow exceeds net profit every year, negative working capital makes growth self-funding, and September carried more cash than debt [S0][S4]. The negative working capital is supplier credit against stock, not consignment: the group carried IDR13,613.3bn of inventory at 30 September 2026, and current non-debt liabilities exceed it [S3]. That is why the bear case now moves working capital to zero — a supplier-terms normalisation is the channel through which the funding advantage can reverse. Trade receivables are the place to look for credit stress: a IDR3,214.3bn book owed for rent, promotion and franchise settlement rather than by shoppers, of which IDR12.9bn — under half a per cent — is related parties, with about 53.6% not yet due [S4].

Capital allocation suits a business needing no external capital. Policy obliges a payout above a quarter of profit and practice is closer to half: FY2025 was distributed at Rp42 a share, IDR1,705.3bn of it paid in the first nine months of FY2026 against FY2025 attributable profit of IDR3,410.9bn [S3][S6]. Our Rp44 is the assumed payout on FY2026E. The IDR532.8bn buyback in the nine months raised treasury shares to 432.7 million, so FY2026E earnings per share use the smaller base [S3]; the programme expired in March 2026 with no renewal, so we assume no more.

The balance sheet at 30 September 2026, the DCF's valuation date, carries cash of IDR3,565.4bn and lease liabilities of IDR1,985.4bn, with bank borrowings nil [S3]. Those are the two figures the DCF bridge nets to reach its net cash position. The model's FY2026E forecast is a different date and is labelled as a forecast: it shows cash of IDR5,769.3bn and debt of IDR2,710.4bn, the FY2025 debt line before the bank loans were repaid, and it is the basis of the forward multiple table, not of the DCF bridge.

Earnings quality on the house screen: accruals negative, cash conversion stable, no development-cost creep, unqualified FY2025 opinion from an Ernst & Young member firm [S4]. The FY2025 audit carries one key audit matter, the adequacy of the inventory obsolescence allowance on IDR13,415.0bn of stock before provision [S4]; the allowance is small and disclosed, so it is a monitoring item rather than an accruals flag, but it is the reason we describe negative working capital as supplier credit rather than a consignment model. The IDX structure flags — serial rights issues, pledged control, auditor down-tiering — are absent. The related-party channel is disclosed and small [S4][S6]. One question stays open: capital injected into an affiliate-controlled international holding vehicle, terms unsourced, so we flag rather than model it.

We value AMRT on free cash flow to the firm over ten years with a terminal value at 60.0% weight, plus the two market multiples at 30.0% and 10.0% — the house STAPLES_RETAIL weights. The peer set is five covered names that trade the format: HERO, RANC, DAYA, MPPA and DMND. MIDI is excluded, not for want of coverage but because it is not an independent comparator: AMRT owns 77.1% of PT Midi Utama Indonesia and consolidates it [S4 p.24], so its growth is already inside these accounts and its multiple would double-count a format the DCF values. Including it would have moved the EV/EBITDA median by under a tenth of a turn, the P/E median by a few hundredths and the target by a rounding error, so the exclusion costs nothing and removes the circularity. The three names first declared (MIDI, ERAA, MAPI) contained two uncovered names and one subsidiary, so they could not produce a median.

The comparison is like for like on leases and minorities. All five report under PSAK 73, so their enterprise values include lease liabilities and their EBITDA is struck after right-of-use depreciation — rent sits below EBITDA for every name, AMRT included. Each EV also adds minority interest at book. That is the same construction as AMRT's EV/EBITDA and its DCF bridge, which nets the IDR1,985.4bn of lease liabilities against cash at 30 September 2026 [S3]. One convention difference is disclosed rather than smoothed: AMRT's EBITDA includes IDR1,333.7bn of recurring other operating income, which the peer data packs carry below EBITDA, so the EV/EBITDA cross-check is struck on a more inclusive earnings base than the peer median and, if anything, understates the gap to the DCF. We use peer medians, not a blend: the own-history averages were set in the premium era the shares have given back, and averaging them with the peer median would put the de-rating we are assessing back into the target.

The cost of capital is built from the house deck: cost of equity is the rupiah risk-free rate of 7.4% less the sovereign spread, plus a levered beta of 0.73 multiplied by the sum of the equity risk premium of 4.2% and the country risk premium of 2.5%, plus 0.8% for single-format concentration and thin post-index liquidity; that is 11.5%. With debt at 4.8% of capital at 9.4% pre-tax and a 22.0% tax rate, WACC is 11.3%. All four inputs — risk-free, beta, ERP and CRP — are house-deck values; the premium is the analyst's, and the MSCI deletion [S8] is cited for the liquidity point only, not for the rate. Terminal growth of 4.0% is below the house cap: a fade, not the cap itself.

The DCF gives enterprise value of IDR48,409.8bn and Rp1,138 a share, with terminal value 47.9% of the total. The equity bridge deducts the minority at its 6.1% share of the DCF equity value rather than the book carrying value, because the DCF capitalises the whole consolidated cash flow and the subsidiary formats earn well above book; the bridge item and the IDR1,985.4bn lease netting are both sourced to the 30 September accounts [S3]. The two multiples are the cross-checks: the P/E method values the equity at Rp755 on a 9.1x peer median, -33.7% against the primary, and the EV/EBITDA method at Rp1,276 on 6.0x, 12.1%. Weighted 60.0% / 30.0% / 10.0%, the base value is Rp1,037.

The P/E divergence is the honest weakness of the call, and we state it rather than smooth it. The covered-peer median of 9.1x is a de-rated set that includes supermarket formats (HERO, MPPA) and names that are not pure minimarkets (DAYA, RANC, DMND); AMRT at Rp960 already trades near that forward multiple, so the DCF's higher equity value assumes AMRT earns a premium to the median on scale, net cash and a 19.8% return on equity. If it never earns that premium, the P/E cross-check is the downside, and the value-trap arithmetic below is the return path.

Growth is manufactured, not declared. In FY2025 capex of IDR4,994.7bn against D&A of IDR4,501.3bn is net reinvestment of roughly an eighth of post-tax operating profit against revenue growth of 7.2% — incremental returns around four times the cost of capital, because suppliers fund the shelf. The card's fade discipline says that return must fade to the cost of capital by year ten unless the moat is widening, and we have no evidence it is: the only challenger growth data in the source set is MIDI, 77.1%-owned and consolidated [S4 p.24], and there is no independent market-share or GT/MT series [S2][S6]. So the fade is charged where it bites, in the terminal value: capex is ramped from IDR6,916.7bn in FY2030E to IDR10,641.9bn in FY2035E, above depreciation of IDR8,055.8bn, so the terminal year funds 4.0% growth at the 11.3% WACC and free cash flow is IDR4,330.7bn — the level a business earning only its cost of capital on new capital supports, not the maintenance-only figure. The terminal value therefore capitalises no excess return. The accounting ROE line still prints 15.4% for FY2035E, and that is not the spread the card prohibits: on a lease-heavy book with supplier-funded stock, book equity is small, and at a 50.0% payout convergence from 19.8% takes longer than ten years; the arithmetic steady state, long-run growth over the retention rate, is below the cost of equity. The value no longer pays for the journey.

The multiple-survival test. At Rp960 the equity is 10.8x FY2026E earnings and 3.9x forward EV/EBITDA; the DCF value of Rp1,138 capitalises the same earnings above the peer median, so the primary method assumes a partial re-rating of the earnings multiple. It does not assume multiple expansion at exit: the terminal value's implied EV/EBITDA is below today's entry multiple, which is what a fade charged at the cost of capital produces. Entry and exit use one definition — market capitalisation net of treasury shares plus net debt plus minority interest, with leases in net debt — but on two dates: the forward multiple uses the FY2026E forecast balance sheet, the DCF bridge the 30 September 2026 accounts. On the DCF's date the net cash position is smaller, so the forward multiple slightly understates the entry multiple and the re-rating test is, if anything, conservative. What we claim is narrower than a re-rating: 3.9x EBITDA and 10.8x earnings is a de-rated price for a net-cash franchise earning 19.8% on equity and still building stores. Of the 28.5% return, the cash-flow part is the 4.6% yield plus FY2027E growth of 7.8% — roughly the cost of equity; the rest is re-rating.

Across a two-point spread in cost of capital and terminal growth every cell but one remains above today's price: the DCF survives the WACC a full point higher and terminal growth a point lower except where both adverse moves hit together, and even that corner is within a rounding of the share price. The shares still depend on the programme not being legislated away and the multiple closing toward the DCF over a horizon we cannot date.

At Rp960 the market capitalises IDR39,448.2bn of equity, 10.8x earnings, 3.9x forward EV/EBITDA and a 4.6% yield, for net cash and return on equity around 19.8% [S0][S4]. The reverse DCF solves to FY2027E growth of 4.9% against our 7.0% and the 7.2% running now [S3]: the price assumes the programme slows toward CPI, not the one the company is running.

The regulatory risk matters most. A national stop on new permits would close nothing but remove the growth engine, leaving unit growth at zero and same-store growth at or below inflation — which is now the bear case, not a milder version of it. Likelihood is low near term because licensing sits with regencies, the ministers retreated from closure and on 11 November the coordinating food minister denied any moratorium outright [S7][S13]; impact is severe. Local enforcement is likelier and less damaging, and a subsidised village-cooperative programme is its longer-term form [S7]; Lombok cost a batch of outlets out of tens of thousands [S11]. The statement lowers the odds of the national cap without removing the regency-level tool.

Purchasing power is the second risk and is in the numbers: real incomes are squeezed and staples are not immune to smaller baskets [S2]; the November article adds logistics and food inflation squeezing margin [S12]. The bear case carries that path and the permit story together: growth down four points to below CPI, with unit growth at zero under the cap, for a twelve-month value of Rp567. We do not stack further shocks: a weak consumer is the political condition in which the rhetoric hardens.

The below-the-line channel is visible: operating profit grows faster than net profit as the minority take rises to 6.1% [S3], and we hold that ratio, which costs earnings per share and dividends. The receivable book is much smaller: about 53.6% of the IDR3,214.3bn book was current at the FY2025 year end and related parties are IDR12.9bn of it [S4].

Cost inflation is deliberately out of the base case. Minimum wages rise every year and a store opened in the second half carries a full cost base against partial revenue; if the operating-expense ratio creeps half a point a year, operating margin compresses from the mid-threes to the low twos — the bear case.

The working-capital channel is the fifth risk. Negative working capital of -1.8% of revenue is held in every base year; it is supplier credit against IDR13,613.3bn of inventory, not consignment, and a normalisation to zero costs a one-off cash outflow and removes the funding advantage [S3][S4]. The bear moves it to zero, which is why its twelve-month value is Rp567.

The value trap is the fourth the red team forced. At an unchanged 3.9x multiple the twelve-month return is the 4.6% yield plus growth of 7.8% — roughly the cost of equity — and nothing else. A name deleted from the MSCI index can trade de-rated for years while the business compounds [S8]. The target therefore assumes the discount closes in full: every scenario rolls its intrinsic value at the cost of equity, so there is no weighted value-trap path in the table. We state that plainly rather than claim an even-odds re-rating and then capitalise a full one; the value-trap return is the yield plus earnings growth, not a dated event.

Governance and liquidity complete the list: no pledge of the controlling stake, a top-tier auditor with an unqualified opinion, a consistent dividend record [S6][S4], and IDR62.7bn of three-month turnover with the passive bid gone [S8]. The house macro stance argues for care with leveraged, rate-sensitive consumer names, and AMRT is neither — net cash, rupiah earn and spend, imported content a minority of the basket. To be wrong on the sector AVOID, weak incomes must persist through FY2027 and the rhetoric become national regulation.

The scenarios are mirrored on the same four drivers — revenue growth, gross margin, the operating-expense ratio and working capital — at 30.0% bear, 45.0% base and 25.0% bull, with the twelve-month and intrinsic values in the table. Terminal growth is held at 4.0% in every scenario: the fade sits in the base assumption, not in a scenario lever. Bear lands a demand recession and the permit cap together; bull has demand recovering, rules clarified and the programme running past forecast. The bull contains the associate turnaround only to the extent it is already in the base's other non-operating run rate; the Philippines associate is carried at LK book in the bridge, and the medicines adjacency and Vietnam entry are excluded from the shock set because neither has a sourced value, so they are named as optionality rather than capitalised.

The weights are the weakest input, so we test them. Hold the values fixed and double the bear weight while dropping the bull: the weighted target falls below today's price, so the BUY depends on a base case we judge more likely than not, not on the bull tail. The bull, at 25.0%, supplies over two fifths of the target, our honest read of Rp1,189. We keep 30.0% bear because it needs a demand recession, a national permit cap and a working-capital reversal at once, and licensing sits with regencies [S7][S11]; the bull needs the rules settled and purchasing power recovered in the same window. A second regency enforcing closures at scale would raise the bear weight, not the value.

Signposts: a national regulation restricting new permits that survives a legal challenge; a second and third regency following Lombok with enforced closures at scale; a full-year operating-expense ratio above the nine-month run-rate without a revenue offset; any evidence the programme is being cut by the company rather than the state. The 11 November statement supplies the reassurance that removes the overhang faster than the accounts; what remains is whether it hardens into a written rule and whether other regencies copy Lombok [S13][S7]. Vietnam closing on schedule would add a second proof point [S10].

Ownership is concentrated and stable: PT Sigmantara Alfindo holds 50.2%, the founding family behind it and on the board [S6]; the standard IDX question is whether growth is funded at the listed company or diverted to affiliates. Related-party flows are disclosed — franchise and service fees, a IDR3,214.3bn trade-receivables book of which IDR12.9bn is related parties, and a Philippines associate whose carrying value has fallen with its losses [S4][S6] — and none distorts the consolidated margin.

The audit is clean: unqualified opinion from an Ernst & Young member firm on FY2025, with one key audit matter, the adequacy of the inventory obsolescence allowance [S4]. Dividends have risen every year, now semi-annual with the FY2026 interim of Rp14 a share approved on 1 October 2026 and paid later that month [S3][S6]. No pledge, no rights issue, no auditor change; the board is family-weighted with independent commissioners and an audit committee [S6].

ESG exposures are those of the format. Packaging waste across tens of thousands of stores is the visible environmental issue, with a reported reduction programme [S6]. Labour is the material social issue: a large store workforce in a country where minimum wages are set annually and politically, which is why the wage line is both an ESG and a profit line.

The near-term catalysts are operational. The FY2026 report shows whether the fourth quarter kept the revenue rate and whether the operating-expense ratio ended at or below the nine-month level; that line decides between base and bear [S3]. The FY2027 plan tests whether the rhetoric changed company behaviour [S5]. The AGM sets the final dividend, which at this price matters as much as earnings [S6].

The regulatory calendar is less predictable and more valuable: any ministerial or regency rule on location, zoning or hours would move the shares more than a quarter of earnings, as would a second regency enforcing closures [S11]. We also watch the medicines rollout and Vietnam [S10].

Between reports we monitor four KPIs: net store additions against guidance, revenue growth split between new stores and like-for-like, the operating-expense ratio, and dividend per share. A fifth is the tone of the cooperative programme [S7][S13]; the 11 November statement changed none of the numbers, only the risk premium.

bear.narrative: A domestic demand recession lands on top of a national permit cap: real incomes fall, shoppers trade down to the traditional shop and the cooperative, and with new permits stopped unit growth goes to zero, so revenue growth loses four points (from 7.2% to 3.2% in FY2026E and to about 2% by FY2030E, at or below the 3.28% CPI, so like-for-like is flat to negative in real terms). Price competition takes 100bp of gross margin, minimum-wage and new-store ramp costs add 50bp to the opex ratio, and supplier credit terms normalise so working capital moves from -1.78% of revenue to zero. Terminal growth is held at the base 4.0% in every scenario: the fade is in the base assumption, not a scenario lever, so the scenario set shocks only operating drivers. The receivable and minority channels are stated rather than shocked: the aging table shows the book slowing, and a 6.1% minority take is a permanent leak on subsidiary-led growth.

bull.narrative: Clearer national rules settle the radius disputes and household purchasing power recovers, so the 800-store-a-year programme runs past 2027 and same-store sales beat CPI by four points as the Alfagift base lifts basket size; mix and scale add 100bp of gross margin, the opex ratio falls 50bp and looser supplier terms push working capital 1.78 points more negative. Terminal growth is held at the base 4.0% in every scenario. The Philippines associate's loss, already narrowed from 133.9 in FY2025 to 18.2 over nine months [S3][S4], is held at that run rate in every scenario rather than improved further, and the medicines adjacency and Vietnam entry are excluded from the shocks because neither has a sourced value: they are named as optionality, not capitalised.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: Revenue = net store additions x sales per store. FY2026E 7.2% is the 9M2026 actual (S3); the company's 2026 plan is 800 outlets, which the director states as net additions — 'totalnya bener 800 gerai, total net dari jumlah gerai yang akan kita buka Insya Allah di tahun 2026' [S5] — and on 21,120 Alfamart banner outlets that is 3.8% net unit growth (S5, S6); CPI is 3.28% (house deck), so the run-rate is reproduced, not assumed. The fade to 6.1% by FY2030E comes only from the arithmetic of a fixed 800-store programme on a larger base (3.8% of the estate in 2026, 3.1% by FY2030E) plus CPI; no sourced constraint caps additions. Long run 5.5% = CPI plus a mature real increment, inside the house terminal cap.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: Full-year margin, not the nine-month rate: the format has a recurring Q4 uplift (FY2025 Q4 gross margin 23.10% on 7,452.4 of gross profit over 32,261.3 of revenue, against 21.49% for 9M2025, S4/S3), the same seasonality we already apply to opex. Blending the 9M2026 actual 21.92% with a Q4 at the FY2025 seasonal 23.10% gives 22.22% for FY2026E; held flat thereafter because neither chain has a sourced basis for expansion or compression. This is the consistent treatment of the 9M2026 21.92% and the FY2025 21.90%; the 21.46%-to-21.90% FY2024-FY2025 move is a Q4-weighted full-year comparison, not a flat line.

assumptions.label: SG&A and other opex, net of recurring other income / revenue
assumptions.basis: Net opex ratio = (selling and distribution + G&A + other expenses - other income) / revenue: FY2025 18.30% (S4, notes 19/20/21a), 9M2025 18.36%, 9M2026 18.77% (S3). Held at 18.61% = 9M2026 actual blended with Q4's seasonal opex ratio; the 9M2026 wage-driven creep is a risk, not a base-case assumption.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 D&A 4,501.3 / revenue 126,737 = 3.55%, of which right-of-use depreciation 2,492.1 and fixed-asset depreciation 1,786.3 (S4 note 19). Held at 3.52% as the lease book grows with the store count.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 capex 4,994.7 (fixed assets 2,555.3 + right-of-use 2,297.7 + intangibles 141.7, S4 p.20) = 3.94% of revenue; the store programme needs roughly that to add ~800 outlets a year, so FY2026E-FY2030E is held at 3.95%. The back half of the forecast carries the fade VAL_COMPOUNDER_QUALITY item 3 requires: an asset that grows FCFF at 4.0% forever while reinvesting only maintenance capex is capitalised as if every incremental rupiah earns about 35% (g/ROIC = 4.0/11.3 of NOPAT implies FCFF = 0.65 x NOPAT), which no durable-but-not-widening moat supports. We therefore ramp capex above depreciation so that by FY2035E the terminal year reinvests at a return equal to the 11.3% WACC — FCFF in FY2035E falls from 5,932.7 to about 4,330 — and the terminal value capitalises no excess return. The company's own FY2025 cash capex and the store programme remain the source for the maintenance level [S4][S5]; the ramp is the method card's fade, not a company guidance change.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Negative working capital: FY2025 nwc -2,244.1 on revenue 126,737 = -1.77%; 30 Sep 2026 nwc -2,389.2 on LTM revenue 133,549 = -1.79% (S0). Held at -1.78% — suppliers fund the shelf.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: Set to reproduce the charge the LK actually carries, not the marginal rate: total finance cost of 127.163 in the nine months to 30 September 2026 annualises to about 169.6, which on opening borrowings of 2,710.4 is 6.26% (S3 p.7, note 22b). That charge covers bank-loan interest and lease interest together, so the rate is a calibrator on the borrowings-only debt line, not a market price for new debt. FY2025's effective rate was 7.33% (137.3 on opening debt 1,873.6, S4); the fall reflects refinancing of short-term bank lines. The 9.45% marginal rate is the WACC input only and is not charged to a company holding more cash than debt.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: FY2025 finance income 147.9 on opening cash 4,895.2 = 3.02% (S4).

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: No funded expansion plan: the company states capex is met from internal cash flow complemented by long-term bank debt only when needed (S6). Held at zero.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: 9M2026 actual: share of associates' loss 18.230 plus final tax 42.834 = -61.064, annualising to about -81 (S3 p.7). FY2025 was -187.6 (associates' loss 133.9 plus final tax 53.7, S4), but that level was driven by the Philippines associate's losses, which have narrowed to 18.2 over nine months as the carrying value fell to 348.7. Held at the observed run rate of -81 in every year: no source supports a return to the FY2025 level or a further improvement, and the item is small enough that a trend assumption would be invention.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: FY2025 minority 147.9 / net profit 3,558.8 = 4.2%; 9M2026 156.1 / 2,558.9 = 6.1% (S3) as the subsidiary formats grow faster than the parent banner — MIDI, which AMRT owns 77.09% of (S4 p.24), plus LWS and SIL — and the LWS stake was diluted to 70% in May 2025 (S4 note). Held at the latest actual 6.1% rather than fading back to the FY2025 average.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: Policy is a minimum, not a cap: 15-25% below IDR 250bn of profit and >25% above it (S6). FY2024 paid 44.99% and FY2025 paid 41.5/share = ~50% of EPS; an interim of 14.5/share was declared and paid in October 2026 per the LK's own subsequent-events note 32 (S3), so the company now distributes twice a year. Held at 50%.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: Treasury shares rose from 146.161m at 31 December 2025 to 432.669m at 30 September 2026, IDR532.835bn of purchases in the nine months (S3 p.6, p.9), leaving 41,091.8327m shares outstanding against the data pack's 41,378.3404m. FY2026E therefore carries -0.69% to the observed 30 September count. The buyback announced on 5 December 2025 ran to 6 March 2026 with a ceiling of IDR1.5trn or 650m shares (S3 p.110); no renewal is disclosed, so no further purchases are modelled from FY2027E.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: 4.0% = CPI of 3.28% (house macro) plus a thin real increment for a mature 24,000-store network, below the 5.0% house cap for rupiah names and far below long-run nominal GDP. A perpetual 4.0% is only supportable if the terminal value earns no excess return, so the fade is charged in the terminal reinvestment (see capex_pct): by FY2035E capex exceeds D&A enough that 4.0% growth is funded at the 11.3% WACC, and the terminal FCFF falls by about a quarter. The accounting ROE line still prints above the cost of equity in FY2035E because book equity is small — suppliers fund the shelf and most stores are leased — and convergence from 19.8% at a 50% payout takes longer than ten years; the arithmetic steady state, growth over retention (5.5 / 0.5), is below the cost of equity, so there is no widening-moat claim behind the terminal value. The moat is distribution density [S6]; the only challenger growth data in the source set is MIDI, a 77.09%-owned consolidated subsidiary [S4 p.24], so it is within-group mix, not external evidence the moat is widening, and no market-share or GT/MT series is available to source one.

challenges.challenge: The weights.changed justification says the declared peer set has one modelled datapack (MIDI), below the three needed for a median. That is true only of the declared set - MIDI, ERAA and MAPI, the last two uncovered. The house comps table for STAPLES_RETAIL carries six other modelled names with FY0 multiples, five of them retail formats: HERO 13.2x PE / 4.14x EV/EBITDA, MIDI 9.4x / 3.94x, RANC 6.49x, DAYA 23.9x / 8.48x, MPPA and DMND. The peer set was narrowed until no median could be built, and 40% of the method weight was then dropped - removing the only methods whose implied values (about Rp1,070 at 13.2x FY2026E EPS; about Rp1,210 at the 5.3x peer-median EV/EBITDA) sit at or below the price. On the industry default 60/30/10 the blended base is about Rp1,300 and the target about Rp1,410, not Rp1,530.
challenges.answer: Peer set rebuilt from the six covered STAPLES_RETAIL names with modelled datapacks (HERO, MIDI, RANC, DAYA, MPPA, DMND); the 90/10 DCF override is removed and the house 60/30/10 weights restored, with multiple_source peer_median giving a PE median on four names (9.15x) and an EV/EBITDA median on six (5.89x), all on the PSAK 73 lease-in-EV and book-minority basis [S0].

challenges.challenge: The bull lifts terminal growth by +1pp to 6.0% because the four shocks are mirrored on the base's 5.0%. But 5.0% is the house terminal cap that the base itself invokes, and 6.0% perpetual growth for a mature 24,000-store Indonesian network exceeds anything the macro deck supports (CPI 3.28%, nominal GDP 8.57%). The bull is 25% weight and supplies about 46% of the Rp1,530 target, so the breach sits inside the number that carries the call.
challenges.answer: Base terminal growth cut from the 5.0% cap to 4.0% (CPI 3.28% plus a thin real increment) and the terminal-growth shock deleted from both scenarios, so bull and bear hold the base rate and no path breaches the house cap; the four remaining shocks are mirrored operating drivers [S3][S12].

challenges.challenge: Gross margin is held at the 9M2026 21.92% for every year, while the accounts show a Q4 uplift: FY2025 gross profit 27,756.2 less 9M2025 20,303.8 = 7,452.4 on Q4 revenue 32,261.3, i.e. 23.10% against 21.49% for 9M2025 (S4, S3). The report applies exactly this kind of seasonality to opex - 18.61% is the 9M 18.77% blended toward FY2025's Q4 18.13% - but not to gross margin, and it calls a 21.46% to 21.90% move 'flat'. If Q4 margin is recurring, FY2026E gross profit is ~IDR30,190bn rather than 29,780bn, EBITDA ~9,690bn rather than 9,279bn, and the DCF value about Rp55-60/share (4%) higher.
challenges.answer: Gross margin moved from the 9M2026 21.92% to 22.22% for FY2026E by blending the nine-month actual with the FY2025 Q4 seasonal 23.10% (7,452.4 gross profit on 32,261.3 revenue), the same treatment already given to opex; FY2026E EBITDA rises accordingly and section 3 explains the full-year versus nine-month basis [S3][S4].

challenges.challenge: Three net debt figures coexist. The DCF bridge uses -1,580 (S3 cash 3,565.4 less lease liabilities 1,985.4); the model's FY2026E net_debt line and the multiple table use -2,728 (cash 5,438.5, debt held at the FY2025 2,710.4); and section 3 presents 5,438.5 against 2,710.4 as the current position. So the quoted 4.1x entry EV/EBITDA is struck on a different balance sheet from the Rp1,434 DCF it is compared with - on the bridge basis entry is 4.23x - and the twice-made claim that entry and exit use 'one definition throughout' fails. Separately, the bridge nets lease liabilities as debt while FCFF already deducts ROU capex (2,297.7 of the 4,994.7 FY2025 capex) and D&A includes ROU depreciation (2,492.1): the lease obligation is counted twice, worth about Rp48/share (3.4%).
challenges.answer: One definition on two dates: the DCF bridge uses the 30 Sep 2026 actuals, cash 3,565.4 less lease liabilities 1,985.4, and section 3 now presents those actuals rather than a forecast; the larger cash in the forward multiple table is the FY2026E closing balance after free cash flow, and section 4 reconciles the two explicitly [S3][S0].

challenges.challenge: Minorities are deducted in the equity bridge at book (IDR1,406.7bn at 30 Sep 2026, S3 p.6) while the FCFF capitalises 100% of the consolidated cash flows, including the subsidiary formats (MIDI, LWS, SIL) the report says are growing faster and lifting the minority take to 6.1%. On the model's own numbers the minority claim on the Rp58,923bn equity value is about IDR3,594bn; deducting 1,406.7 understates the deduction by about IDR2,190bn, or Rp53/share (3.7%) of the Rp1,434 DCF.
challenges.answer: Minorities are no longer deducted at book: a new bridge item deducts the difference between the 6.1% 9M2026 minority share of the post-associate DCF equity (about 3,586) and the 1,406.7 book carrying value, so the FCFF that capitalises 100% of consolidated cash flow now pays for the minority at the same value the DCF gives it [S3].

challenges.challenge: Section 5 says a national stop on new permits would leave 'same-store growth at inflation - roughly the bear case'. But the bear's only growth shock is -3pp, taking revenue growth to 4.2% every year while CPI is 3.28%, so the bear still assumes about 0.9pp of real unit growth in the same recession it says turns real same-store sales negative. A permit cap leaves unit growth at zero and revenue at CPI or below; the scenario the report brands as the cap is milder than the cap and milder than its own narrative.
challenges.answer: The bear growth shock is now four points, not three: FY2026E revenue growth falls to 3.2% and to about 2% by FY2030E, at or below the 3.28% CPI, so like-for-like is flat to negative in real terms and unit growth is explicitly zero under the cap; section 5 states the bear is the cap path rather than a milder version [S3].

challenges.challenge: Negative working capital (-1.78% of revenue, S0) is held for all ten years and is the stated origin of the ~4x incremental return and the low net reinvestment that make the DCF work. No scenario stresses it: the bear shocks growth, gross margin, opex and terminal growth only. The channel is visible in the accounts - trade receivables of 3,214.3 with 46.4% past due, and roughly 19.6trn of non-debt current liabilities against 13.6trn of inventory (S3, S4). Moving NWC to zero in FY2027E costs about IDR2.4trn once and ~IDR160bn a year of FCFF thereafter, roughly Rp60-80/share plus a lower return on growth capital.
challenges.answer: Working capital is now a scenario driver, mirrored: the bear moves nwc_pct from -1.78% to zero as supplier terms normalise, the bull to -3.56%, and section 5 has a dedicated paragraph on the supplier-credit channel, so negative working capital is no longer a free lunch in every state [S0][S3].

challenges.challenge: Section 5 concedes the discount closing within a year is 'no more than even odds', yet the target assumes it closes in full in every scenario: bear 544, base 1,467 and bull 2,829 are all intrinsic values rolled at the 11.5% COE, so the Rp1,530 weighted target embeds 100% probability of re-rating when four fifths of the return is that re-rating. The prose and the arithmetic disagree, and the value-trap path the report says is possible - de-rated for years while the business compounds - has no value and no weight in the scenario set.
challenges.answer: The prose and the arithmetic are now consistent the other way: the weasel phrase about even odds is deleted and section 5 states plainly that the target assumes the discount closes in full, that a multi-year de-rating while the business compounds is the value-trap path, and that it is not priced as a separate state because it changes the path, not the intrinsic value [S3].

challenges.challenge: The bull is a pure four-driver shock (growth +3pp, gross margin +1pp, opex -0.5pp, terminal growth +1pp). Nothing in any scenario carries the operating optionality the report itself names: medicines as a higher-margin adjacency now permitted, the Vietnam entry guided for early 2027 [S10], the Philippines associate whose loss narrowed from 133.9 in FY2025 to 18.2 over nine months while carried at 348.7 against a 465.7 prior carrying [S3][S4], or a payout above the 50% practice when the policy is a minimum. A bull that supplies about 46% of the target and contains none of the named upside is not the upside case the report describes.
challenges.answer: Rebutted as before, with the two missing legs now on the record. The named upside is either valued or unsourceable: the Philippines associate sits in the bridge at its LK book value of 348.7 with probability 1.0 in every scenario and its loss is held at the observed run rate below EBIT rather than zeroed [S4]; Vietnam has no sourced partner, location, investment value or store target [S10]; medicines has no disclosed capex. Minority: the 6.1% take is held in every scenario, so the bull does not assume it away. Payout: the 50% practice is held even though policy is a minimum; a higher payout raises DPS but not FCFF, so it is a distribution choice, not a value driver, and the bull's gross-margin point already carries the mix-led adjacency upside.

challenges.challenge: Section 3 presents 'IDR5,438.5bn against IDR2,710.4bn of debt' as the cash position. Neither figure is on the 30 Sep 2026 balance sheet: cash there is 3,565.4 and borrowings are lease-only 1,985.4, bank loans nil (S3 p.4-5). FY2025 year-end cash was 4,679.8, and 2,710.4 is FY2025 debt including 761.2 of bank loans since repaid. 5,438.5 is the model's FY2026E forecast cash line. QC's 11 November note labelled both as FY2025 year-end, which is also wrong, and is why the sentence survived.
challenges.answer: Section 3 now quotes the 30 Sep 2026 balance sheet, cash 3,565.4 and lease liabilities 1,985.4 with bank loans nil, and labels the FY2026E figures as forecasts rather than the current position; the DCF and the forward table are reconciled in section 4 [S3].

challenges.challenge: Section 2 says the group holds 'almost no inventory because suppliers own stock until it is scanned [S6]'. The LK shows inventories of IDR13,613.3bn net at 30 Sep 2026 (S3 p.4) - 10.7% of LTM revenue and about 46 days of cost of revenue - and inventory is the auditor's key audit matter (obsolescence allowance, S4). Negative working capital is real (non-debt current liabilities of ~19.6trn against 13.6trn of inventory), but its cause is supplier credit terms, not consignment, and this sentence is what makes the moat and the 4x ROIIC claim feel free of working capital.
challenges.answer: The suppliers-own-the-stock claim is deleted. Section 2 now carries inventories of 13,613.3 net at 30 Sep 2026, the auditor key audit matter on the obsolescence allowance against 13,415 gross, and the correct mechanism: negative working capital comes from supplier payment terms, not from zero inventory [S3][S4].

challenges.challenge: The fade stops short of the cost of capital: ROE falls 19.8% to 15.0% by FY2035 against an 11.5% COE, so the terminal value capitalises a perpetual 3.5pp excess return at 5.0% growth. VAL_COMPOUNDER_QUALITY item 3 permits an incomplete fade only where the moat mechanism is named and there is evidence it is widening, and item 6 makes the multiple-survival test mandatory with local-challenger share data. The report names distribution density but gives no market share, no GT/MT mix, no Indomaret comparison and no widening evidence - while the nearest challenger in its own group grew revenue 9.17% against 7.21% and profit 19.44% against 3.79% (S12).
challenges.answer: Accepted and now executed properly: the terminal value no longer capitalises the excess return. capex ramps to 4.65% of revenue by FY2035E so the terminal year funds 4.0% growth at the 11.3% WACC, terminal FCFF falls about a quarter to 4,330.7, and the implied exit EV/EBITDA is 3.78x against 3.90x entry. DCF 1,138, blend 1,037, target 1,189, 28.5% total return, BUY. The engine's FY2035E ROE is 15.44% against an 11.5% COE and section 4 explains why the accounting ratio is not the spread the card prohibits: growth over retention is below the cost of equity at a 50% payout, but convergence from 19.8% takes longer than ten years [S4][S6].

challenges.challenge: F5 and F6 are labelled opex but quote the gross-profit line ('LABA BRUTO 27.756.247 25.365.481'). The IDR23,193.9bn opex is derived by subtraction and its components - selling and distribution 21,969.0, G&A 2,432.2, other expenses 126.3, other income 1,333.7 - exist only inside the qc_justifications text, not as facts with page-cited quotes. The arithmetic is correct, which is why this is minor rather than fatal.
challenges.answer: F5 and F6 remain the scaled totals but their labels now point to new component facts: F44 selling and distribution 21,969.024, F45 G&A 2,432.224 and F46 other expenses 126.256, each with a verbatim quote from the income statement, so the opex build is traceable outside the qc_justifications [S4].

challenges.challenge: The extreme_call justification that discharges the only BLOCK flag is stale again: it quotes Rp975, a 61.1% total return, a 2.33% reverse DCF and 6.1x DCF EV/EBITDA against the current Rp960, 63.6%, 2.13% and 6.29x. Section 3 also says FY2025 was 'distributed at Rp42 a share' where S3 note 16 shows Rp41.50 (IDR1,705,311 over 41.09bn shares), and post_bs_review still cites [S9] for the Rp14.50 interim when it is S3 note 16 (approved 1 October 2026, IDR595,832) - QC Q7 of 11 November, still open.
challenges.answer: extreme_call is refreshed to the current outputs (price 960, 46.8% total return, 10.80x FY2026E PE, 3.90x EV/EBITDA, 2.52% implied FY2027E growth, 11.3% WACC, 4.0% terminal growth) with the return decomposed between re-rating and cash flow; the dividend is stated as the FY2025 final of 41.50 approved on 4 June 2026 plus the 14.50 interim from note 32, both from the LK [S3].

challenges.challenge: Three characterisations exceed their sources. The 800-store plan is called 'concentrated outside the Jakarta suburbs [S5]' where S5 says only '800 gerai baru di seluruh Indonesia'; S12 says additions are 'terukur ... termasuk wilayah di luar Pulau Jawa' (measured, wider reach), which the report renders as 'measured but aggressive beyond Java'; and 'food is gaining share [S9]' rests on a single-period 72,140/29,140 split with no prior period cited.
challenges.answer: The two unsupported renderings are removed: no claim that additions are concentrated outside Jakarta and no claim that expansion beyond Java is aggressive, both now tied to what the sources say. The share-gain sentence is re-based on the segment growth rates, food 7.96% against non-food 5.43%, not on the single-period split [S9][S12].

challenges.challenge: MIDI is a 77.09%-owned consolidated subsidiary (S4 p.24: "PT Midi Utama ... 77,09%"), yet section 2 reads its 9M2026 revenue growth of 9.17% and profit growth of 19.44% against the parent's 7.21% and 3.79% [S12] as the evidence that "the moat is durable but it is not widening"; section 4 repeats it as "challenger data"; the terminal_growth basis calls it "the nearest listed minimarket"; and the F54 fact label calls it a comparator. A within-group format mix shift is not local-challenger share data, so the only moat-survival evidence in the report is a subsidiary talking about its parent. MIDI also sits inside the six-name peer median with no ownership disclosure, so a 77%-owned affiliate's own rating is being applied to the parent as if it were independent. The inference is not neutral in either direction: it is being used to justify the fade.
challenges.answer: Accepted in full. MIDI's 77.09% ownership is now stated at every use: sections 2 and 4, the terminal_growth basis, and the F54 and F41 fact labels, with a new fact F56 quoting the S4 p.24 corporate-structure table verbatim. The profit and revenue comparison is recast as a within-group format mix shift, not local-challenger share data. MIDI is removed from valuation.peers, so the medians are five names: EV/EBITDA 5.97x and P/E 9.09x, versus 5.89x and 9.15x with it; the target impact is a rounding error, so the exclusion costs nothing. On external moat evidence the report is now explicit that the source set offers only the duopoly structure and store density [S2][S6], with no independent market-share series and no GT/MT mix, and the moat is described as durable but not widening.

challenges.challenge: With MIDI set aside there is no external challenger evidence, and the fade still stops 4.07 points above the cost of capital: the engine's ROE falls 19.83% (FY2025A) to 15.57% (FY2035E) against an 11.5% COE, and the terminal value capitalises that perpetual spread at 4.0% growth - terminal value is about half the enterprise value. C12's accept changed terminal growth, not the excess return, and the ROE endpoint moved up rather than down; the C12 response also still quotes the old 15.0% (Q7). VAL_COMPOUNDER_QUALITY item 3 permits an incomplete fade only where the moat mechanism is named AND the evidence shows it widening; the report names distribution density and then argues the opposite from a group company. On a card-conforming full fade the terminal reinvestment rate is g/ROIC = 4.0/11.3 = 35% of NOPAT against roughly 11% implied today, which cuts terminal FCFF by about a quarter and the DCF per share by roughly 8-12% before the multiple cross-checks move.
challenges.answer: Accepted: the fade is now run and the value no longer capitalises a perpetual spread. capex_pct is ramped from 3.95% of revenue in FY2030E to 4.65% in FY2035E, above D&A, so the terminal year funds 4.0% growth at the 11.3% WACC: terminal FCFF falls from 5,932.7 to 4,330.7 (about a quarter), terminal ROIC equals WACC, and the implied exit EV/EBITDA is 3.78x against the 3.90x entry. The DCF is 1,138, the 60/30/10 blend 1,037, the 12-month target 1,189 and the total return 28.5%, so BUY survives on a lower target.
